danish.title: Tiende bog (1812) — Kapitel 33
paragraphs: Slagets hovedhandling ved Borodino udspillede sig på de syv tusinde fod mellem Borodino og Bagrations flècher. Uden for dette område fandt der på den ene side en demonstration sted af russerne med Uvarovs kavaleri ved middagstid, og på den anden side, hinsides Utitsa, Poniatowskis sammenstød med Tutsjkov; men disse var isolerede og svage kampe i sammenligning med det, der fandt sted i centrum. Det var på sletten mellem Borodino og flècherne, tæt ved skoven, på det stykke åbent og synligt terræn fra begge sider, at slagets egentlige afgørelse faldt — på den simpleste og mest brutale måde.
Slaget begyndte fra begge sider med en kanonade fra flere hundrede kanoner.
Derefter, da hele marken var dækket af røg, rykkede to divisioner, Campans og Dessaix', frem fra den franske højre fløj, mens Murats tropper rykkede mod Borodino fra venstre.

Fra Sjevardinoredouten, hvor Napoleon stod, var der godt en kilometer til pileskanserne og over halvanden kilometer i luftlinje til Borodino. Han kunne ikke se, hvad der skete derhenne, så meget mindre som røgen blandede sig med tågen og skjulte hele terrænet. Soldaterne fra Dessaix’ division, der rykkede frem mod skanserne, kunne man kun se, til de nåede lavningen mellem dem og skanserne. Så snart de var gået ned i den, blev røgen fra kanon- og musketilden på skanserne så tæt, at den skjulte hele tilgangen fra den side. Gennem røgen anede man noget sort – antagelig mennesker – og nu og da glimtede en bajonet. Men om de bevægede sig eller stod stille, om det var franskmænd eller russere, kunne man ikke se fra Sjevardinoredouten.

Solen var stået klart op, og dens skrå stråler ramte Napoleon lige i ansigtet, da han med hånden over øjnene kiggede mod flècherne. Røgen lå bredt foran dem, og snart så det ud, som om røgen bevægede sig, snart som om tropperne bevægede sig. Ind imellem hørtes råb gennem røgen, men det var umuligt at afgøre, hvad der foregik derhenne.

Napoleon, der stod på bakken, kiggede gennem en kikkert, og i dens lille cirkel så han røg og mænd — snart sine egne, snart russere. Men når han igen kiggede med det blotte øje, kunne han ikke afgøre, hvor det, han havde set, befandt sig.
Han gik ned fra bakken og begyndte at gå frem og tilbage foran den.
Nu og da standsede han, lyttede til skydningen og stirrede intenst ud over slagmarken.

Men ikke blot var det umuligt at se, hvad der foregik, fra det sted, hvor han stod nedenfor, eller fra bakken ovenover, hvor nogle af hans generaler havde taget plads — selv fra selve flècherne, hvor der skiftevis var russiske og franske soldater, levende og døde, sårede og usårede, forskræmte og forvirrede — selv der kunne ingen forstå, hvad der foregik. I flere timers løb, under uafbrudt musket- og kanonild, dukkede der snart russere, snart franskmænd op — infanteri, kavaleri og artilleri — og da de viste sig, tumlede, faldt, skød, stødte sammen, vidste de ikke, hvad de skulle stille op med hinanden, skreg og løb tilbage igen.

Fra slagmarken blev der konstant sendt adjudanter til Napoleon, og ordonnansere fra hans marskalker kom i galop med rapporter om slagets gang, men alle disse meldinger var falske — dels fordi det i kampens hede var umuligt at sige, hvad der foregik i et givet øjeblik, dels fordi mange af adjudanterne ikke nåede helt til selve kamplinjen, men blot viderebragte, hvad de havde hørt fra andre. Desuden forandrede meget sig, mens en adjudant red den halve eller hele mil til Napoleon, og nyheden var forældet, inden den nåede frem. Således kom en adjudant i galop fra Murat med melding om, at Borodino var taget, og at broen over Kolotsja var i franskmændenes hænder. Ønskede Napoleon, at tropperne skulle gå over? Napoleon gav ordre til, at de skulle tage opstilling på den anden side og vente. Men før han gav ordren – ja, næsten lige så snart adjudanten havde forladt Borodino – havde russerne generobret broen og brændt den. Det var netop den træfning, Pierre havde overværet ved slagets begyndelse.

En adjudant kom i galop fra flècherne med et bleg og forskrækket ansigt og meldte til Napoleon, at angrebet var slået tilbage, at Campan var såret, og Davout dræbt; men i netop det øjeblik, adjudanten havde fået besked om, at franskmændene var slået tilbage, var flècherne i virkeligheden blevet generobret af andre tropper — og Davout levede i bedste velgående og var kun lettere forslået. På baggrund af sådanne uundgåeligt falske meldinger gav Napoleon sine ordrer, som enten allerede var udført, før han gav dem, eller som ikke kunne og ikke blev udført.

Marskallerne og generalerne var tættere på slagmarken, men ligesom Napoleon deltog de ikke selv i kampen og kom kun af og til inden for musketskudsvidde. De traf deres egne beslutninger uden at spørge ham og gav ordre om, hvor der skulle skydes fra og i hvilken retning, hvor rytterne skulle galopere hen, og hvor fodfolket skulle løbe. Men deres ordrer blev ligesom Napoleons sjældent fulgt, og da kun halvt. Som regel gik det stik imod ordren. Soldater, der skulle rykke frem, løb tilbage, når de fik kardæskild imod sig. Soldater, der skulle blive stående, fik pludselig øje på russere lige foran sig og styrtede snart tilbage, snart frem. Rytteriet satte uden ordre efter flygtende russere. To kavaleriregimenter galoperede således gennem lavningen ved Semjonovskoje, og da de nåede bakkekammen, vendte de om og galoperede tilbage i fuldt firspring. På samme måde løb fodfolket undertiden helt andre steder hen, end der var givet ordre til. Hvor og hvornår kanonerne skulle flyttes, hvornår fodfolket skulle sendes frem for at skyde, eller rytterne for at ride det russiske infanteri ned – alle den slags ordrer gav de officerer, der var nærmest de pågældende tropper, uden at spørge hverken Ney, Davout eller Murat, endsige Napoleon. De frygtede ingen straf for at handle på egen hånd eller sidde en ordre overhørig. I kamp gælder det jo det dyrebareste, et menneske har, selve livet, og snart synes redningen at ligge i at løbe tilbage, snart i at løbe frem. Mændene midt i kampens hede handlede, som øjeblikket indgav dem. I virkeligheden blev troppernes stilling hverken bedre eller anderledes af al den renden frem og tilbage. At de løb og red løs på hinanden, gjorde kun ringe skade. Det, der lemlæstede og dræbte, var kanonkuglerne og geværkuglerne, som fløj over de marker, hvor mændene tumlede om. Så snart de slap ud af kugleregnen, samlede deres overordnede bag fronten dem igen og bragte dem under disciplin. I kraft af den disciplin førte de dem atter ind i ilden, hvor dødsangsten opløste disciplinen, og hvor enhver fór af sted, som mængden nu tilfældigvis rev ham med.

english.title: Book Ten (1812) — Chapter 33
paragraphs: The main action of the Battle of Borodino took place within the seven thousand feet between Borodino and Bagration's fortifications. Beyond that space, there was on one side a demonstration by the Russians with Uvarov's cavalry at midday, and on the other, beyond Utitsa, Poniatowski's clash with Tuchkov; but these were isolated and minor actions compared to what happened in the center. On the field between Borodino and the fortifications, beside the wood, the main action of the day took place in an open space visible from both sides, and was fought in the simplest, most straightforward way.
The battle began on both sides with a cannonade from several hundred guns.
Then, when the entire field was covered with smoke, two divisions — Compans's and Dessaix's — advanced from the French right, while Murat's troops advanced on Borodino from their left.

From the Shevardino Redoubt where Napoleon stood, the fortifications were about two-thirds of a mile away, and it was more than a mile as the crow flies to Borodino, so Napoleon couldn't see what was happening — especially since the smoke mixing with mist obscured the whole area. The soldiers of Dessaix's division advancing toward the fortifications could only be seen until they had descended into the hollow between them and the defenses. Once they entered that hollow, the smoke from guns and muskets grew so dense it hid the entire approach. Through the smoke, glimpses could be caught of something black — probably men — and now and then the glint of bayonets. But whether they were moving or standing still, whether French or Russian, was impossible to tell from the Shevardino Redoubt.

The sun had risen brightly and its slanting rays struck directly into Napoleon's face as, shading his eyes with his hand, he peered at the fortifications. The smoke spread before them, and at times it looked as though the smoke was moving, at times as though the troops were. Shouts could sometimes be heard through the firing, but it was impossible to tell what was actually happening there.

Napoleon, standing on the knoll, peered through a field glass, and in its small circle saw smoke and men — sometimes his own, sometimes Russians — but when he looked with the naked eye, he couldn't tell where what he had just seen actually was.
He descended the knoll and began pacing back and forth before it.
He stopped occasionally, listened to the firing, and stared intently at the battlefield.

But it was impossible to make out what was happening — not only from where he stood below, or from the knoll above where some of his generals had positioned themselves, but even from the fortifications themselves — where by now there were alternately or simultaneously Russian and French soldiers, dead, wounded, living, terrified, or maddened. Even there it was impossible to tell what was going on. For several hours, amid incessant cannon and musket fire, now only Russians were seen, now only Frenchmen, now infantry, now cavalry: they appeared, fired, fell, collided without knowing what to do with each other, screamed, and ran back again.

From the battlefield, adjutants Napoleon had sent out and orderlies from his marshals kept galloping up with reports on the action's progress, but all these reports were false — both because it was impossible in the heat of battle to say what was happening at any given moment, and because many adjutants didn't go to the actual fighting but reported what they'd heard from others, and also because by the time an adjutant had ridden the mile or more to Napoleon, circumstances had changed and his news was already outdated. For example, an adjutant galloped up from Murat reporting that Borodino had been taken and the bridge over the Kolocha was in French hands. The adjutant asked whether Napoleon wanted the troops to cross. Napoleon gave orders to form up on the far side and wait. But before that order was given — almost as soon as the adjutant had left Borodino — the bridge had been retaken by the Russians and burned, in the very skirmish Pierre had witnessed at the start of the battle.

Another adjutant galloped up from the fortifications with a pale, frightened face, reporting that the French attack had been repulsed, Compans wounded, and Davout killed. Yet at the very moment the adjutant had been told the French were beaten back, the fortifications had actually been recaptured by other French troops, and Davout was alive with only a minor bruise. Based on these necessarily unreliable reports, Napoleon issued orders that either had already been carried out before he gave them, or could not and were not carried out.

The marshals and generals, who were closer to the fighting but, like Napoleon, did not participate in the actual combat and only occasionally came within musket range, made their own decisions without consulting Napoleon and issued orders about where and how to fire, where cavalry should charge and infantry should run. But even their orders were rarely carried out, and then only partially. For the most part, things happened contrary to their commands. Soldiers ordered to advance ran back when met with grapeshot; soldiers ordered to hold their ground suddenly rushed forward or backward when Russians appeared unexpectedly before them, and cavalry charged without orders in pursuit of fleeing Russians. In this way two cavalry regiments galloped through the Semenovsk hollow, and as soon as they reached the crest turned around and galloped back at full speed. The infantry moved the same way, sometimes running to entirely different places than ordered. All commands about moving guns, sending infantry to fire, or dispatching horsemen to ride down Russian infantry were given by the officers on the spot nearest the units, without consulting Ney, Davout, or Murat, much less Napoleon. They didn't fear punishment for disobeying orders or acting on their own initiative, because in battle what's at stake is the dearest thing of all — one's own life — and sometimes safety seems to lie in running back, sometimes in running forward. These men in the thick of battle acted on the impulse of the moment. In reality, however, all these movements forward and backward accomplished little harm on their own; the actual damage — the maiming and killing — was done by the balls and bullets flying over the fields where these men floundered about. The moment they left the zone of fire, their commanders in the rear re-formed them, restored discipline, and marched them back into the killing zone, where, under the influence of mortal fear, they broke discipline again and rushed about at random.
